newsitem.title: CHILE: Enami's doors open to Chilean smelter ventures.
newsitem.headline: Enami's doors open to Chilean smelter ventures.

text.p: Chile's state copper smelting company, Empresa Nacional de Mineria (Enami), now expanding its refinery, would consider future joint-ventures with private companies for new smelter capacity and has had some early talks, an official said Friday.
Sergio Taulis, commercial manager of Enami, said the firm has spoken with companies including Compania Minera Candelaria, a big northern Chilean mine controlled by Phelps Dodge of the United States.

"We have spoken about the subject at my level with people in the commercial area, but I definitely imagine there have been talks at higher levels of the company in which some producers have manifested interest, not only Candelaria," Taulis told Reuters in an interview.

Stressing that talks are still informal and any concrete project still distant, Taulis said that any new increase in Enami's smelting capacity would not necessarily come in the form of an expansion of its two existing smelters. The possibility of a brand new installation would have to be considered.
"It is not easy to determine a priority if it is best to expand an installation located in one particular geographical location of the country or seek an alternative geographical location," he said.

Under its $150-million modernization program, Enami sees its output of refined copper growing to 328,000 tonnes by 1999, or 4.37 percent of world output, from this year's 214,000 tonnes, which give it a 3.19-percent share of the world market.
Its smelted copper output should rise to 204,000 tonnes in 1999, a 2.68-percent world market share, from 190,000 tonnes, or a 2.75-percent share, this year.

But, with the Chilean government wary of allowing state money to be invested in commercial projects, any future Enami expansion will probably have to be funded by private joint-venture partners, Taulis said.

Much of the money of the company's modernization program has been spent on cleaning up its two sulfur-dioxide belching smelters, Ventanas on the coast near the capital Santiago, and Paipote in northern Chile near the Candelaria mine.

The Paipote smelter had provoked the wrath of grape farmers in the Copiapo district. But Enami's clean up program will see 90 percent of its smelter' sulfur emissions eliminated in the next few years, down from 77,700 tonnes a year in 1989.

Another addition to local smelter capacity separate from Enami may be on the way. Chile's National Mining Society said earlier this year that South Korea's Hyundai had commissioned it to carry out a preliminary study on the possibility of installing a $300-600 million smelter in the country.
Apart from running its two smelters, and a copper refinery at the Ventanas complex, Enami also provides aid to Chile's smaller mines.
